title: Codegen and finding your way around locators

parts.title: Codegen and finding your way around locators

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 4 - Fundamentals - Codegen and finding your way around locators

A test can act on an element only after it finds the element. This lesson explains how Playwright
finds elements on a page, which ways of finding them keep working when a page changes, and how a
tool called Codegen suggests them for you.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | How Playwright finds the elements on a page, and how Codegen suggests locators for you. |
| **Goals** | Explain what a locator is, choose a locator that keeps working after a redesign, and record locators with Codegen. |
| **Prerequisites** | The project that you created in [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2). |
| **Tools** | `getByRole`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByText`, and Codegen with the Playwright Inspector. |
| **Environment** | The banking website, signed in as Leela, in the editor on the right and in your own project. |
| **Key takeaway** | Find an element by what a user sees, not by how the page is built. |

## How a web page is built

A web page is written in **HTML**, a language that describes each element on the page. Each element
is written as a **tag**, such as `<button>` for a button or `<input>` for a text field. The HTML of a
page is also called its **markup**.

A **locator** is a piece of code that describes how to find one element on a page. In the examples
below, `page` is the browser tab that the test controls. An **id** is a name that a page gives to
one element, and a **class** is a name shared by elements that look alike. In a locator, `#` before
a name means "the element with this id". Playwright offers several kinds of locator. Some describe
what a user sees, and others describe how the page is built:

| Kind of locator | Example | Keeps working when the page is redesigned? |
|---|---|---|
| id or class | `#ng-x7f2q3` | Often not. Many tools create new ids and classes each time the site is built. |
| **XPath**, a path through the markup | `//div[3]/button[1]` | No. It breaks as soon as the layout changes. |
| `getByRole` | `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })` | Yes. It depends on what the element is and what it says. |
| `getByPlaceholder` | `page.getByPlaceholder('Enter Email')` | Yes. It depends on text that the user sees. |

An element's **role** is the kind of element it is, such as a button, a link, or a heading. Its
**accessible name** is the text that describes it, usually its visible label. A **placeholder** is
the grey hint text inside an empty text field.

These locators work the way a **screen reader** does. A screen reader is a program that reads a page
aloud for people who cannot see it, and it finds elements by role and name, not by markup. Playwright
also offers `getByLabel`, which finds a field by its label, and `getByText`, which finds an element by
the text inside it.

## Codegen and the Inspector

**Codegen**, short for code generator, records what you do in a browser and writes the matching
Playwright code. To start it, open the integrated terminal in your project and run:

```bash
npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/
```

The command opens two windows. One is a browser showing the banking website, and the other is the
**Playwright Inspector**, which shows the code. Then:

1. In the browser window, select the email field and type `leela@gmail.com`.
2. Select the password field and type `Leela@123`.
3. Select **Login**. Each time you click or type in the browser, a new line of code appears in the
   Inspector.
4. Copy any code that you want to keep. Codegen saves nothing.
5. Close both windows. Codegen keeps the terminal busy while it runs, so if the prompt does not
   come back, click in the terminal and press **Ctrl+C**.

**Explanation:** The Inspector shows a whole test file. Read only the lines that begin
`await page.`, because each of them is one step that you performed. The rest of the file is
explained in [Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2).

Codegen chooses `getByRole` and `getByPlaceholder` whenever it can, for the reasons in the table
above. Treat what it writes as a first draft. It records every click, including clicks you did not
mean to make, so keep the locators and remove the rest.

variation.prompt: After signing in, select Transaction History on the dashboard, and show a screenshot of the page that opens. The items on the dashboard are text, not links, so use page.getByText('Transaction History') to find it.

blocks.text:
## Why the name of a test file matters

Playwright runs only the files whose names match its pattern for test files. By default, that means
names that end in `.spec.ts` or `.test.ts`. A file named `login.ts` is never run, even if it contains
a correct test. Playwright shows no error and no warning for it. [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3)
proves this in your own project.

## Best practices

- Choose `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByPlaceholder`, or `getByText` before an id, a class, or an
  XPath.
- Use Codegen for a first draft, then keep the locators and remove the clicks you did not mean.
- Name every test file so that it ends in `.spec.ts`.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Named a test file without `.spec.ts` | Its tests never run, and no error appears | Rename the file so that it ends in `.spec.ts`. |
| Copied everything Codegen recorded | The test works, but contains clicks that do nothing useful | Keep the locators, and remove the extra steps. |
| Used `getByRole('link', ...)` for an item on the dashboard | The locator finds nothing | On this website, the items on the dashboard are text, not links. Use `getByText`. |
Why does Codegen write `getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })` instead of `#ng-x7f2q3`?

options: Because Playwright can find an element by its role faster than by its id
Because the role and the name survive a redesign of the page
Because an id can match more than one element on the same page
checkpoint.explanation: Many tools create a new id such as `#ng-x7f2q3` each time the site is built. The button is still a button, and it still says Login, so a locator based on its role and name keeps working.

blocks.text: You save a test in a file named `login.ts`. What happens when you run your tests?

options: Playwright stops with an error about the file name.
Playwright runs the test and reports it as skipped.
Playwright never runs the test, and shows no error.
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright runs only files whose names end in `.spec.ts` or `.test.ts`. It ignores `login.ts` completely, without an error or a warning. [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3) proves this in your own project.

blocks.text: How should you use the code that Codegen writes?

options: As a first draft: keep the locators, and remove the extra clicks
As finished code that you paste into a test file without any change
As an example to read, after which you type your own locators from memory
checkpoint.explanation: Codegen records every click, including clicks you did not mean to make. Its locators are useful, so keep them, and remove the steps that the test does not need.

blocks.text:
- A **locator** is code that describes how to find one element on a page.
- Choose `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByPlaceholder`, or `getByText`. They depend on what a user sees.
- An id, a class, or an XPath depends on how the page is built, and often breaks after a redesign.
- Codegen writes a first draft. Keep its locators, and remove the extra steps.
- Playwright runs only files whose names end in `.spec.ts` or `.test.ts`.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3) proves the naming rule by creating a test file without the
`.spec.ts` ending and watching Playwright ignore it.

# Week 1 - Day 4 - Implementation - Proving the `.spec.ts` naming convention

In [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2), you read that Playwright ignores a test file whose name does not
end in `.spec.ts`. In this lesson, you prove it in your own project: you create a correct test file
with the wrong name, watch Playwright ignore it, and then rename it.

You do every step in VS Code and in its integrated terminal, in the project that you created in
[Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Proving in your own project that Playwright ignores a test file with the wrong name. |
| **Goals** | Watch Playwright ignore a correct test file, then find it after a rename, and check which tests Playwright can see. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2), where you read about the naming rule. |
| **Tools** | `npx playwright test --list`, which lists the tests without running them. |
| **Environment** | VS Code and its integrated terminal, in your project folder. |

## Step 2: List the tests that Playwright can see

The `--list` option makes Playwright list the tests that it would run, without running them. In the
terminal, run:

```bash
npx playwright test --list
```

**Output**

```output
Listing tests:
  [chromium] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [chromium] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
  [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [firefox] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
  [webkit] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [webkit] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
Total: 6 tests in 1 file
```

**Explanation:** The list contains only the two tests from `example.spec.ts`, once for each browser.
The new test is missing, although its file is in the `tests` folder and its code is correct.
Playwright shows no error and no warning about it.

## Step 3: Rename the file

In the Explorer panel, right-click `not-a-spec.ts`, select **Rename**, change the name to
`not-a-spec.spec.ts`, and press Enter. Then run the same command again:

```bash
npx playwright test --list
```

**Output**

```output
Listing tests:
  [chromium] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [chromium] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
  [chromium] › not-a-spec.spec.ts:3:5 › the login page shows an email field
  [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [firefox] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
  [firefox] › not-a-spec.spec.ts:3:5 › the login page shows an email field
  [webkit] › example.spec.ts:3:5 › has title
  [webkit] › example.spec.ts:10:5 › get started link
  [webkit] › not-a-spec.spec.ts:3:5 › the login page shows an email field
Total: 9 tests in 2 files
```

**Explanation:** Nothing inside the file changed. Only its name did, and now Playwright finds the
test and lists it once for each browser. A name that ends in `.test.ts` works in the same way.

## Step 4: Clean up

In the Explorer panel, right-click `not-a-spec.spec.ts` and select **Delete**, so that your project
contains only the example tests again.

## Why this matters

Most mistakes in a test show up as a failure. A wrongly named file shows up as nothing at all: every
run passes, because the test never runs. When a test seems to have disappeared, run
`npx playwright test --list` and count what Playwright can see.

## What a reviewer looks for

- Every test file ends in `.spec.ts`.
- When a test seems to be missing, the reviewer lists the tests before reading any code.
`--list` reports `Total: 6 tests in 1 file`, but your `tests` folder contains two files. What does this tell you?

options: One of the files contains a mistake, so Playwright skipped its tests.
Playwright does not see one file, most likely because of its name.
The tests in one of the files are switched off until you enable them.
checkpoint.explanation: A mistake in the code causes an error that you can see. A file whose name does not end in `.spec.ts` or `.test.ts` adds nothing to the list, and no message explains why. Check the file names first.

blocks.text: After the rename, the total went from 6 tests to 9. Why?

options: Only the name changed, and Playwright chooses files by name
The rename added the test to a list of files that Playwright keeps
Playwright corrected the code in the file as part of the rename
checkpoint.explanation: Not one character of the code changed. Playwright decides which files to read from their names alone. It then listed the new test once for each of the three browsers, which added three to the total.

blocks.text:
- Playwright chooses which files to run from their names, before it reads any code.
- A file with the wrong name is ignored, without an error or a warning.
- `npx playwright test --list` lists the tests that Playwright can see, without running them.
- When a test seems to be missing, list the tests and count them.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w1/d4/p4) has you use Codegen yourself, and repeat this experiment from the
beginning.

# Week 1 - Day 4 - Practice - Codegen and locators

These three problems use Codegen and the locators from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2), and the
naming rule from [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3). You run Codegen and the test commands in your own
project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems about Codegen, locators, and the naming rule, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2) for Codegen and locators, and [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3) for the naming rule. |
| **Environment** | Your own project for Codegen and the test commands, and the editor on the right for your answers. |

## How to answer

Select **Start this in the editor** to open a template for a problem, and write your answer on the
lines that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution** to compare it with a model answer.

## When you are done

You can now find elements with locators that keep working when a page changes, and check which test
files Playwright can see. In [Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), you learn the parts of the
language that every test uses.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A record of the locators that Codegen writes for you. In the integrated
terminal in your project, run:

```bash
npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/
```

Sign in with the email `leela@gmail.com` and the password `Leela@123`, then select **Pay Bills** on the
dashboard. Copy the lines that the Inspector shows into the template.

**Where.** Codegen runs from your terminal. Write your answer in the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** Every line in your answer was copied from the Inspector, not
typed from memory.

**What to build.** A short explanation of why `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })`
keeps working after a redesign, when `#ng-x7f2q3` or `//div[3]/button[1]` may not. A
**redesign** is a change to how a page looks and how its markup is arranged. Name one change
that a redesign often makes, and say how it affects each of the three locators.

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** Your answer names a specific change, such as a new container
around the button, rather than saying only that the page changed.

**What to build.** The experiment from [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3), repeated from the
beginning with a test that you write yourself. In your project:

1. In the `tests` folder, create `practice-broken.ts`, with one test that opens the banking
   website and checks that the Login button is visible.
2. Run `npx playwright test --list`, and note the total.
3. Rename the file to `practice-broken.spec.ts`, run the same command, and note the total again.
4. Delete the file.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Write your test and the two totals in the
editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The total changed between the two runs, and you saw it change
in your own terminal.

**Hint.** Start from the test in [Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3), and replace its check with one
on `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })`.
